intro: Open your backpack and read the tags. Your things came from all over the world. Now walk outside. The road, the streetlight and the library down the block were not bought by any one person. We paid for them together.

This unit is about how people work together. First you will learn why people and countries trade. You will see what Illinois sells and buys, and how Chicago moves goods. Then you will learn about taxes, public goods and the jobs people do.
By the end, you will be able to tell an import from an export. You can figure out a sales tax. You can sort public and private goods. You can also make a plan for a job you wonder about.
bigQuestion: How do trade, taxes and work connect us to our community and the world?

timeline.t: Adam Smith publishes The Wealth of Nations, explaining why people trade
The U.S. Constitution gives Congress the power to collect taxes
David Ricardo explains how countries gain by making what they do best and trading
The Illinois and Michigan Canal opens, linking Lake Michigan to the Illinois River
The Chicago Board of Trade is founded to trade grain
The 16th Amendment lets Congress collect a national income tax
The National Park Service is created to care for national parks
The Social Security Act is passed to help older people
Congress passes a law to build the Interstate Highway System
The St. Lawrence Seaway opens, so ships can sail from Chicago to the ocean

words.d: giving something to get something else you want
focusing on making one thing or doing one job that you do well
a good made in one country and sold to people in another country
a good brought into a country from another country to be sold
when people or places depend on each other for goods and services
a tax on goods brought in from another country
money people and businesses must pay to the government to pay for shared services
something many people can use at once, where it is hard to stop anyone from using it
something you buy that you use, so others cannot use the same one
work that one person does for someone else, like teaching or fixing a road
the money a worker is paid for work, often counted by the hour
the skills and knowledge a person has that help them work

test.q: Corn grown in Illinois is sold to Japan. For the United States, the corn is:
test.why: Goods that leave the country to be sold are exports.

test.q: Phones made in another country are sold in Chicago. For the United States, they are:
test.why: Goods that come into the country are imports.

test.q: In one hour, Ana can make 10 cards or 2 bracelets. Jo can make 3 cards or 6 bracelets (example). Who should make bracelets?
test.why: Jo makes 6 bracelets an hour and Ana makes 2, so Jo should make bracelets.
A tariff is a tax on goods brought in from another country.

test.q: A shirt costs $20 with a 5% sales tax (example). What is the total?

test.why: Shoes are bought and used by one person, so they are a private good.

test.q: Why does Chicago matter for trade?
choices: It makes all the world's phones
Many rail lines, a busy airport and a port meet there
test.why: Chicago's trains, O'Hare and the port move goods to and from many places.

test.q: A storm closes a port, and a store runs short of bikes. This shows:
test.why: The store depends on goods from far away. That is interdependence.

test.q: Who is a government worker paid with taxes?
test.why: Public school teachers are paid mostly with tax money.

test.q: A town can fix a bridge or build a new playground, not both. This is a:
test.why: Choosing one means giving up the other. That is a trade-off.

test.q: A worker earns $15 an hour (example) for 4 hours. How much does she earn?
Which group works to help people, not to make money for owners?
test.why: A nonprofit works for a cause, not profit for owners.

test.q: What usually happens to pay when many businesses need a skill few people have?
test.why: When many employers want few workers, they offer more pay.

test.q: What does the U.S. Constitution give Congress the power to do?
test.why: Article I, Section 8 gives Congress the power to lay and collect taxes.

test.q: Learning a skill in a training program builds your:
test.why: Skills and knowledge you learn are your human capital.

write.prompt: Your town has $50,000 (example). It can fix the roads near the port so trucks move goods faster, or it can open the library on Sundays. Choose one. Use numbers and words from this unit to explain your choice and what the town gives up.
tips: Say which one you choose in your first sentence.
Name the trade-off: what does the town give up?
Tell who is helped: buyers, sellers, workers or readers.
Use at least two words from this unit, like trade, tax or public good.
